artiest/louis-barron.text:
Louis Barron was an American pioneer of electronic music, born in Minneapolis in 1920. As a young man he enjoyed working with soldering irons and electrical equipment. He studied music at the University of Chicago. In 1947 he married Bebe Barron, and the couple moved to New York. A cousin who worked at 3M gave them their first tape recorder as a wedding present. With it they began to experiment with sound on magnetic tape. In 1950 they made Heavenly Menagerie, the first electronic music for magnetic tape composed in the United States.

Louis built electronic circuits, above all with a ring modulator, that produced sounds and patterns that were unique and unpredictable. He made the recordings, while Bebe combed through hours of tape and shaped the compositions from it. In 1952 and 1953 John Cage used their studio for his first tape piece, Williams Mix, for which the Barrons recorded more than six hundred sounds. It was Cage who convinced them that their sounds were music. In 1956 they composed the first fully electronic film score, for MGM's Forbidden Planet. Because of a dispute with the musicians' union, the credits did not carry the intended word music but read electronic tonalities instead.

The music for Forbidden Planet sounded eerie and ominous, and unlike anything the audience had heard before. In doing so, Louis and Bebe Barron pointed the way to electronic sounds in film, pop music and later synthesizers.
artiest/louis-barron.listen: Listen to the music from Forbidden Planet and notice the pulsing, humming sounds that belong to no recognisable instrument. Can you hear how each theme has its own electronic colour?

artiest/louis-en-bebe-barron.text: Louis and Bebe Barron were a married couple with their own electronic studio in New York. There they experimented with tape recorders and home-built circuits. They also worked on tape pieces by John Cage. Louis built electronic circuits that made sounds until they burned out. Bebe and he recorded these and processed them with reverb, echo, filters and tape manipulation. With this technique they made the soundtrack for Forbidden Planet (1956) for MGM. It was the first fully electronic film score, years before the synthesizers of Moog and Buchla. Because they were not members of the musicians' union, their work was credited as 'electronic tonalities' and could not compete for an Oscar.
artiest/louis-en-bebe-barron.listen: Notice that no ordinary instruments sound: only glowing, gliding and pulsing electronic sounds that sit somewhere between music and sound effect.

artiest/louis-jordan.text:
Louis Jordan was an American saxophonist, singer, songwriter and bandleader. He was born in Brinkley, Arkansas, in 1908. His father was a music teacher and the leader of a brass band, and as a child Louis learned the clarinet and then the saxophone. As a teenager he played with the Rabbit Foot Minstrels, a travelling show. In the 1930s he worked in Philadelphia and New York, singing and playing alto saxophone in Chick Webb's orchestra alongside Ella Fitzgerald. In 1938 he started a group of his own, the Tympany Five.

In the 1940s Jordan became the king of the jukebox. With hits such as Is You Is or Is You Ain't My Baby, Five Guys Named Moe, Caldonia and Choo Choo Ch'Boogie he reached number 1 on the black music charts eighteen times, and he also scored with a white audience. He recorded duets with Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald and Louis Armstrong and appeared in short musical films. His band was small, five or six musicians, but played as hard as a big band. Saturday Night Fish Fry (1950) was one of the first popular songs with the word rocking in the chorus and a distorted electric guitar.

Jordan made jump blues: fast, swinging dance music that blended jazz, blues and boogie-woogie, with funny lyrics about city life. In this way he laid the foundations of rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll. Producer Milt Gabler used his records as a model for Bill Haley, and Chuck Berry borrowed guitar licks from Jordan's guitarist Carl Hogan. Jordan died in 1975.
artiest/louis-jordan.listen: Listen to Saturday Night Fish Fry and notice the call-and-response singing between Jordan and his band. Listen too for the short guitar licks played on two strings at once: exactly the kind of riff Chuck Berry would later take over.

artiest/louis-jordan-and-his-tympany-fiv.text:
Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five was an American rhythm and blues and jazz band, founded in 1938 by Louis Jordan. Jordan played alto, tenor and baritone saxophone and sang most of the songs. He had started out with the Elks Rendezvous Band, named after a jazz club in Harlem. The Tympany Five consisted of a horn section of three to five players, with drums, double bass, guitar and piano. The name says five, but the line-up often included two or three extra players.

The group made many songs that later became defining for early rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll, including Let the Good Times Roll, Keep A-Knockin' and Caldonia. In 1941 it was moved at Decca from the so-called race series to the Sepia series, intended for artists who could appeal to both a black and a white audience. Jordan was always proud that his music was popular with both groups.

The music is swinging dance music for a small group. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame calls him the father of rhythm and blues and the grandfather of rock 'n' roll. Chuck Berry said that Jordan was the first person he heard play rock 'n' roll. Carl Hogan's opening riff in Ain't That Just Like a Woman returns in Johnny B. Goode.
artiest/louis-jordan-and-his-tympany-fiv.listen: Listen to Caldonia and notice the lively, fast singing and the short riffs of the horns. How does the band respond to the singer?

artiest/louis-moholo.text:
Louis Tebogo Moholo, later also known as Louis Moholo-Moholo, was a South African jazz drummer, born in 1940 in Langa, Cape Town. From the late 1950s he played in South African bands, including Ronnie Beer's Swinging City Six, and in 1962 he performed at the Cold Castle National Jazz Festival. He then formed the Blue Notes with pianist Chris McGregor, Johnny Dyani, Nikele Moyake, Mongezi Feza and Dudu Pukwana. In 1964 the group emigrated to Europe, for the Antibes jazz festival. In 1965 the musicians settled in London, where they formed part of a South African community in exile that made an important contribution to British jazz.

Moholo played in Brotherhood of Breath and in Assagai, and worked with many innovators of free jazz, including Derek Bailey, Steve Lacy, Evan Parker, Cecil Taylor, Archie Shepp and Peter Brötzmann. His first album under his own name was Spirits Rejoice. Others followed, including Tuned Boots in 1978, Human Aspect in 1990 and Mpumi in 2002. In 2005 he returned to South Africa. He died in Cape Town in 2025.

Moholo brought the energy of South African township jazz to European free jazz. His playing is powerful and full of rhythmic shifts, and he showed how African singing and melodies can be combined with improvisation.
artiest/louis-moholo.listen: Listen to a recording of Spirits Rejoice and notice how the drums do not merely keep time but speak along with the horns like a voice of their own. Can you hear how rhythm and melody flow into one another?

artiest/louis-moholo-moholo.text: The drummer Louis Moholo was born in Cape Town and played in Chris McGregor's The Blue Notes, with whom he left for Europe in 1964. In London he played in Brotherhood of Breath and with free improvisers such as Evan Parker and Irène Schweizer. He led groups of his own such as Spirits Rejoice and Viva-La-Black. His playing connects free European improvisation with the rhythms of South African jazz. After the end of apartheid he returned to South Africa in 2005 and added a second Moholo to his name. He was the last surviving member of The Blue Notes and died in 2025.
artiest/louis-moholo-moholo.listen: Hear the drums, which are free and danceable at the same time.

artiest/louis-prima.text:
Louis Prima was an American trumpeter, singer, entertainer and bandleader, born in New Orleans in 1910 into a musical Italian-American family with Sicilian roots. He first learned the violin, but became interested in jazz when he heard black musicians such as Louis Armstrong. In the late 1920s he formed a seven-piece band in the New Orleans style. In the 1930s he led a swing combo, and in the 1940s a big band. In 1936 his New Orleans Gang played at the Famous Door club in New York.

In 1948 he met the singer Keely Smith. In 1954 they began an act together at the Sahara in Las Vegas, with saxophonist Sam Butera and his group The Witnesses. It proved a hit and led in 1955 to a contract with Capitol Records. There The Wildest! was released in 1956, containing among other things a medley of Just a Gigolo and I Ain't Got Nobody. The Call of the Wildest followed in 1957 and Louis and Keely! in 1959. Prima mixed jazz and swing with early R&B, rock 'n' roll, boogie-woogie and Italian folk music such as the tarantella, and liked to use Italian words in his songs. He also lent his voice to the orangutan King Louie in Disney's 1967 film The Jungle Book. He died in 1978.

Prima showed that ethnic background in jazz and pop could be an asset rather than a handicap. His Las Vegas show brought jazz and entertainment close together.
artiest/louis-prima.listen: Listen to Just a Gigolo / I Ain't Got Nobody and notice the raw, playful singing and the band's jump swing. Can you hear how he turns a melancholy song into a party?

artiest/louis-silvers.text:
Louis Silvers, known as Lou Silvers, was born in New York in 1889 as Louis Silberstein. He became an American composer of film music whose work was used in more than two hundred and fifty films. He wrote the music for the sound sequences of D. W. Griffith's 1921 film Dream Street, at a time when film was still silent and sound was a novelty. In 1927 he composed and conducted the music for The Jazz Singer, the film regarded as the first with spoken and sung parts, which heralded the transition to sound film.

His best-known song is April Showers from 1921. In 1935 he won the first Academy Award for Best Original Score, for the film One Night of Love. For most of the long run of Lux Radio Theater, from 1934 to 1955, he was also the musical director of that radio programme.

In this way Silvers links the pop and revue song with the American film industry. He worked in the period when film, radio and popular music began to find one another, and he showed that a songwriter could also be a film composer. He died in 1954 in Hollywood, of a heart condition.
artiest/louis-silvers.listen: Listen to April Showers and notice how the melody evokes the rain and the hope in the chorus at the same time. Can you hear how simple and singable the line is?

artiest/louis-van-dijk.text:
Louis van Dijk, also written Louis van Dyke, was one of the best-known Dutch pianists, with a career of more than fifty years in jazz and classical music. He was born in Amsterdam in 1941 as Arnold Ludwig van Dijk. His father was the sexton of the Prinsessekerk, where he heard the organist Piet van Egmond play. In 1959 he entered the Amsterdam Conservatory, where he studied piano with Jaap Callenbach. As early as 1961 he won the Jazzconcours, and in 1964 he graduated cum laude in classical piano. He developed, however, as a jazz pianist, with Oscar Peterson, Bill Evans and Bud Powell as his great examples.

For years Van Dijk worked with Ramses Shaffy and Liesbeth List in the ensemble Shaffy Chantant. Later he often played with Pim Jacobs and Pieter van Vollenhoven as Gevleugelde Vrienden. His records appeared in the form of a trio, quartet or quintet, and with, among others, Toots Thielemans, Thijs van Leer, Rogier van Otterloo and the Rosenberg Trio. That list includes titles such as Louis van Dyke Plays Lennon-McCartney from 1970, Bluesette from 1972 and Sketches on Bach from 1974.

Van Dijk was known for his talent for improvisation, even within the classical repertoire. He showed how Bach, the Beatles and jazz can come together on one piano. He died in Laren in 2020.
artiest/louis-van-dijk.listen: Listen to Sketches on Bach and notice how he takes over a Baroque melody and plays a jazz rhythm and improvisations of his own around it. Can you hear where Bach ends and Van Dijk begins?

artiest/loulou-tielman.text:
Loulou Tielman was the drummer of the Tielman Brothers, the first Indo-Dutch band to break through internationally. He was one of the children of Herman Tielman, who came from Kupang on the island of Timor, and Flora Lorine Hess. Together with his brothers Andy, vocals and guitar, Reggy, guitar, and Ponthon, bass, he had already performed in Indonesia, under the names Timor Brothers and The Four T's. In the mid-1950s the family came to the Netherlands. They settled first in Breda and later in The Hague.

The brothers stood out for their wild performances. They threw guitars to one another and played the bass with their teeth. At the 1958 World's Fair in Brussels they were allowed to step in briefly between the sets of a Hawaiian band, and they made such an impression that they were asked to play clubs in Germany, including on the Reeperbahn in Hamburg. In that same year Rock Little Baby of Mine was released, which is regarded as the first Dutch rock 'n' roll single. In Germany the Tielman Brothers became one of the most popular live acts; in the Netherlands they received far less attention. Their biggest Dutch hit came only in 1967, with Little Bird.

The Tielman Brothers were at the origin of indorock, a blend of Western rock 'n' roll and Indonesian music. In their wake many other Indo bands moved to Germany. Later the family left for Australia. Loulou Tielman died in 1994.
artiest/loulou-tielman.listen: Listen to Rock Little Baby of Mine by the Tielman Brothers from 1958 and notice how Loulou's drums and the guitars push the rhythm forward together. Remember that this was the first Dutch rock 'n' roll single, made by a band that had only just arrived from Indonesia.

artiest/ltj-bukem.text:
LTJ Bukem, real name Daniel Andrew Williamson, is a British jungle producer and DJ, born in 1967. He and his label Good Looking are above all associated with the jazzy, atmospheric side of jungle. He was trained as a classical pianist and discovered jazz fusion as a teenager. At one point he played in a jazz-funk band. In the late 1980s he chose DJing, and he became known in the rave scene of the early 1990s. His stage name comes from his nickname Book 'em, taken from the television series Hawaii Five-O.

With his label Good Looking Records and the club Speed in London, which he ran with DJ Fabio, he carved out a place of his own. The compilation series Logical Progression revealed a side of drum and bass influenced by jazz and ambient. That style became known as intelligent drum and bass. In 1995 he made an Essential Mix together with MC Conrad. In 1997 he remixed the James Bond theme for David Arnold's project. Only in 2000 did his first solo album appear, the double album Journey Inwards, which leaned heavily on his love of jazz fusion.

Bukem plays all over the world, often under the name Progression Sessions. He shows that a fast breakbeat and soft piano chords can together create a calm, almost meditative atmosphere, and in this way he gave dance music a side that could be listened to.
artiest/ltj-bukem.listen: Listen to a track from Journey Inwards and notice the fast breakbeats beneath soft, jazzy piano chords and flowing synthesizers. Can you hear how those two layers do not get in each other's way?

artiest/lucas-debargue.text:
Lucas Debargue is a French pianist and composer, born in Paris in 1990. He grew up in Compiègne in a family without musicians: his mother is a nurse and his father a physiotherapist. He had his first piano lesson at the age of ten. At fifteen he gave up the piano, because he had become more interested in literature. At seventeen he moved to Paris, where he studied literature and art. In 2010 he played again at the Fête de la Musique festival in Compiègne. He then met the piano teacher Rena Shereshevskaya, and from 2012 he studied with her at the École Normale de Musique de Paris. In that period he decided to become a professional musician.

In 2015 he took part in the fifteenth International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow, where as a complete unknown he caused great excitement with an idiosyncratic programme that included Nikolai Medtner's first sonata. He won fourth prize and signed with Sony Classical that same year. His recordings include Bach, Beethoven and Medtner from 2016, Quatuor pour la fin du temps from 2017, 52 Sonatas from 2019 and a complete edition of Fauré's solo piano music from 2024. He plays in halls such as the Philharmonie de Paris, Carnegie Hall, Wigmore Hall and the Concertgebouw.

Debargue shows that a late start and a detour through literature can lead to a personal sound. His playing is expressive and his programmes are often unexpected.
artiest/lucas-debargue.listen: Listen to his recording of Fauré's piano music and notice the soft touch and the long, flowing lines. Can you hear how each note is given its own colour?

artiest/lucia-popp.text:
Lucia Popp, born Lucia Poppová, was a Slovak operatic soprano, born in 1939 in Záhorská Ves in what was then Czechoslovakia. Her mother was a soprano, and together they often sang duets at home. She first studied medicine, then drama at the Academy of Performing Arts in Bratislava. Her voice was discovered when she was given a role in Le Bourgeois gentilhomme in which she had to sing. She began as a mezzo-soprano, but her voice acquired a high register, and she began singing as a soubrette, later as a light and lyric coloratura soprano. Her discography includes Die Zauberflöte from 1964, Carmina Burana from 1966, Die lustige Witwe from 1968 and Die Fledermaus from 1976.

In the 1970s she moved from coloratura roles to lyric ones. In the 1980s, as her voice matured, she took on heavier parts, such as the Countess in Mozart's Le nozze di Figaro, the title role in Strauss's Arabella and the Marschallin in Der Rosenkavalier. She performed at the Wiener Staatsoper, the Metropolitan Opera, Covent Garden and La Scala. She also appeared in films, including Jánošík in 1963.

Popp died in Munich in 1993 of brain cancer, at the age of fifty-four. In 2007 she was ranked seventh in BBC Music Magazine's list of the twenty greatest sopranos of all time. Her clear, warm voice showed how a single singer can grow from light to heavy roles.
artiest/lucia-popp.listen: Listen to an aria sung by Lucia Popp from Die Zauberflöte and notice how pure the high notes sound. Can you hear how light and yet powerful her voice is?

artiest/luciano-berio.text:
Luciano Berio was an Italian composer, born in 1925 in Oneglia on the Ligurian coast. His father and grandfather were organists and taught him to play the piano. After the war a hand injury prevented him from continuing as a pianist and he turned to composing, first at the Milan conservatory. There he married the American mezzo-soprano Cathy Berberian, for whom he wrote a great deal of music. Later he studied with Luigi Dallapiccola, met Boulez and Stockhausen among others in Darmstadt, and became a teacher in the United States, including at the Juilliard School.

In 1955 he founded the Studio di fonologia musicale in Milan together with Bruno Maderna, one of the most important studios for electronic music in Europe. There he made Thema (Omaggio a Joyce) in 1958, in which the voice of Berberian reading from James Joyce's Ulysses is manipulated by technical means. Laborintus II won the Prix Italia in 1966. His best-known orchestral work is Sinfonia from 1968. He also wrote the Sequenza series, solo pieces in which instruments and voice are used with extended playing techniques.

Berio also belongs in the history of pop. According to a biography of Lennon and McCartney, McCartney attended a concert of Laborintus 2 in 1966 and afterwards spoke with the composer. The tape collage in that piece is said to have been an inspiration for the Beatles' sound-collage work on Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. Berio died in Rome in 2003.
artiest/luciano-berio.listen: Listen to Laborintus 2 and notice how voices, instruments and tape material are layered over one another. Try to hear where a sound collage emerges of the kind you also know from the pop music of the late 1960s.

artiest/luciano-pavarotti.text:
Luciano Pavarotti was an Italian operatic tenor who, towards the end of his career, also found a large audience in pop music. He was born in 1935 in a council housing estate on the edge of Modena, the son of a baker who himself had a fine tenor voice. As a boy he sang in a choir with his father, became first a schoolteacher and later an insurance agent, and took singing lessons for years. Only when he won the Achille Peri competition in 1961 did he make his debut, as Rodolfo in La bohème in Reggio Emilia.

After that things moved fast. He sang in Vienna, at Covent Garden and, in 1965, in Miami, where he stepped in at the last moment alongside Joan Sutherland. He toured Australia with her. That year he also made his debut at La Scala, under Herbert von Karajan. In 1966 he sang in London as the first tenor to hit nine high Cs in the aria Ah! mes amis. His recordings include complete operas, such as La bohème, Tosca, Turandot and Rigoletto, alongside individual arias and compilation albums such as Mamma and Passione. He excelled in bel canto, the earlier work of Verdi and the operas of Puccini.

In 1990, during the football World Cup, he performed as one of the Three Tenors. The trio's first album became the best-selling classical album ever. Pavarotti also organised benefit concerts for refugees and the Red Cross. His last performance was Nessun dorma at the 2006 Winter Olympics in Turin. He died in 2007.
artiest/luciano-pavarotti.listen: Listen to his recording of Nessun dorma from Turandot and notice how he builds the long, high notes and sustains the phrase. Can you hear how an operatic voice can fill an entire hall without a microphone or amplification?

artiest/luckey-roberts.text:
Luckey Roberts, in full Charles Luckyth Roberts, was born in Philadelphia in 1887 and died in 1968. He was an American composer and pianist in the stride style, which encompasses jazz, ragtime and blues. As a child he was already performing in travelling vaudeville and minstrel shows. At the age of seven he taught himself the piano, but only in F sharp, the key of the black keys. Over a period of about ten years he travelled to Europe three times.

Around 1910 he settled in New York. He became one of the leading pianists of Harlem and often won piano contests, while still having to learn to write down notes. The pianist Artie Matthews helped him with that. In 1911 he wrote The Junk Man Rag, followed in 1913 by Pork and Beans, an early example of stride. Ripples of the Nile dates from around 1912. Other well-known compositions are Moonlight Cocktail and Railroad Blues. He also ran a restaurant and a bar in New York and Washington and gave music and dance lessons.

In stride piano the left hand jumps between bass and chord, while the right hand embellishes. Roberts was a friend of Eubie Blake. In his playing you can hear how ragtime passed into the piano jazz of Harlem.
artiest/luckey-roberts.listen: Listen to Ripples of the Nile and notice the left hand constantly jumping between low notes and chords. Can you hear the fast, almost rippling embellishments in the right hand?

artiest/ludovic-navarre.text:
Ludovic Navarre is a French DJ and producer, born in 1969 in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris. He is best known under the stage name St Germain. As a boy he listened to Bob Marley, Toots & the Maytals, Miles Davis and Kool & the Gang. From 1991 he released techno and deep house under various names, first on FNAC, the label of Laurent Garnier and Eric Morand, and then on their new label F Communications. From 1993 he used the name St Germain for his deep house. That same year, with Garnier and Shazz as Choice, he made the track Acid Eiffel, one of the first French dance hits.

In 1995 his first album Boulevard was released, a deep house record with many jazz influences. Mixmag named it the best album of that year. He was then invited to make an album for Blue Note, the famous jazz label. That became Tourist (2000), with among others Rose Rouge and Sure Thing. The album came out as lounge music was on the rise, sold millions of copies worldwide and earned him an Edison. After that it went quiet for a long time. In 2015 the album St Germain appeared, on which he mixed Malian instruments such as the kora, balafon and ngoni with electric guitars and electronic loops.

Navarre combines house with jazz: a tight dance beat with live-played horns, piano and samples of old jazz and blues records. In doing so he became one of the best-known names of nu jazz, and he showed that jazz and electronic dance music can go well together.
artiest/ludovic-navarre.listen: Listen to Rose Rouge by St Germain and notice the repeated piano figure, the tight house beat beneath it and the voice that keeps repeating the same phrase. Hear how horns and percussion then join in, as if a jazz band were playing along with a DJ.

artiest/ludovico-einaudi.text: Ludovico Einaudi was born in Turin in 1955. He studied composition at the Milan conservatory and graduated in 1982. In that same year he received orchestration lessons from Luciano Berio. At first he wrote classical works in traditional forms, then pieces for dance and multimedia. From the mid-1990s he wrote film music. For Acquario (1996) he received an award for best soundtrack. Filmmakers often use existing pieces by him. For example, Una mattina and Fly are heard in Intouchables (2011) and Nuvole bianche in This Is England (2006). Nomadland and The Father (both 2020) also use his music. His style rests on repeated melodic patterns, with the piano as the main instrument.
artiest/ludovico-einaudi.listen: Listen to how a short piano pattern keeps returning while the melody above it slowly changes, and how strings later make the repetition fuller.

artiest/ludwig-brav.text:
Ludwig Brav was a musician from the world of silent film in Germany. Little else is known about his life in our sources. He worked with Giuseppe Becce and Hans Erdmann, two composers who in the 1920s wrote and compiled music for the cinema. In 1927 the three together published the Allgemeines Handbuch der Filmmusik.

That handbook was intended for the pianists and small orchestras who accompanied a silent film live in the cinema. It built on Becce's Kinothek, a collection of snippets of music, each of which belonged to a particular mood or situation, such as tension, pursuit, despair or a mysterious night. Whoever accompanied the film could thus play in the style and motifs of well-known composers without having to invent everything themselves. The book therefore belongs to the early history of film music in Germany: it records how music colours an image, an idea that later returns in the work of film composers.
artiest/ludwig-brav.listen: Listen to a piece of film music from the silent era, for example from Becce's Kinothek, and notice how in a few bars the music sets a mood such as tension or fear.

artiest/ludwig-goransson.text: Ludwig Göransson (born in 1984 in Linköping) studied in Stockholm and in Los Angeles. He works both as a pop producer, for Childish Gambino among others, and as a film composer. His regular collaboration with the director Ryan Coogler began with Fruitvale Station (2013) and Creed (2015). For Black Panther (2018) he travelled to Senegal and South Africa and incorporated, among other things, the talking drum into an orchestral score with hip-hop beats. He won an Oscar for it. For The Mandalorian (2019) he combined a Western atmosphere with synthesizers. For Oppenheimer (2023) he won his second Oscar, with a score in which a solo violin takes centre stage.
artiest/ludwig-goransson.listen: Notice how Göransson puts one distinctive sonic element at the centre, such as the talking drum or the solo violin, and blends it with orchestra and electronics.

artiest/ludwig-van-beethoven.text: Ludwig van Beethoven came from Bonn and settled in Vienna in 1792, where he took lessons with Haydn. He stretched the classical forms into personal dramas and kept on composing while growing steadily deafer. His Fifth Symphony of 1808 builds an entire work from a single four-note motif and moves from C minor to a radiant C major. In doing so he became the great example for the whole of the nineteenth century.
artiest/ludwig-van-beethoven.listen: Listen to the opening of the Fifth and count how often you hear the four-note motif return, even when it is passed along quietly.

artiest/luis-bacalov.text:
Luis Enríquez Bacalov was born in Argentina in 1933 and died in Rome in 2017. He was an Argentine-Italian film composer and pianist and came from a family of Bulgarian Jews. He learned music from Enrique Barenboim, the father of the conductor Daniel Barenboim. He wrote music that became classic for many spaghetti Westerns, such as Django, A Bullet for the General and The Grand Duel, and for Italian crime films such as Caliber 9. In 1980 he also wrote the music for Fellini's La città delle donne.

Bacalov was nominated for an Oscar in 1967 for his music for Pasolini's film about the Gospel of Matthew, and won the prize in 1996 for Il Postino. In the early 1970s he worked with Italian progressive rock bands such as New Trolls and Osanna. He also wrote for choir and orchestra, including Misa Tango from 1997, a mass set to the rhythms of the tango. He also wrote the first triple concerto for bandoneon, piano, soprano and symphony orchestra. From 2005 he led the Orchestra della Magna Grecia in Taranto.

His Western music reached a large audience through Quentin Tarantino, who used pieces by him in Kill Bill and Django Unchained, including Django itself. In this way the music of an Italian spaghetti Western reached a new audience.
artiest/luis-bacalov.listen: Listen to Django and notice the singing and the accompaniment. What atmosphere does the music evoke?

artiest/luis-fonsi.text:
Luis Fonsi, in full Luis Alfonso Rodríguez López-Cepero, was born in 1978 in San Juan, Puerto Rico. When he was ten the family moved to Orlando, Florida. At high school he sang in an a cappella group that also included Joey Fatone, later a member of *NSYNC. In 1995 he began the music programme at Florida State University on a full scholarship, but he dropped out to focus on his career. He then received a recording contract with Universal Music Latin.

His debut album Comenzaré was released in 1998 and became a hit in Puerto Rico and Latin America. It was followed by, among others, Eterno in 2000, Abrazar la vida in 2003 and Palabras del silencio in 2008. In 2009 he won a Latin Grammy for Song of the Year with Aquí estoy yo. In 2002 he tried to conquer the American market with the English-language album Fight the Feeling.

The worldwide hit came in January 2017 with Despacito, a duet with Daddy Yankee. In April an English remix with Justin Bieber was released. Until 2020 the video was the most-viewed video on YouTube. The music combines Latin American pop with reggaeton, a style with danceable rhythms. In 2017 Fonsi became tourism ambassador of Puerto Rico. With Despacito he showed that a Spanish-language song could top the charts worldwide.
artiest/luis-fonsi.listen: Listen to Despacito and notice how Fonsi and Daddy Yankee alternate. Which rhythm carries the song?

artiest/lukas-vasilek.text:
Lukáš Vasilek is a Czech musician who works mainly with choral and vocal music. He is named as chorus master on the 2014 recording of Leoš Janáček's Glagolitic Mass. It was released on Supraphon, with the Prague Radio Symphony Orchestra and the Prague Philharmonic Choir under Tomáš Netopil.

Of his own recordings the album listings name Testamentum, with choral works, from 2014, Cantatas and Madrigals from 2018, Village Stories from 2023 and Honegger: Jeanne d'Arc au bûcher from 2026. That is a broad repertoire, from madrigals and cantatas to a twentieth-century oratorio.

The Glagolitic Mass shows what such a choral work demands. Janáček wrote it in 1926 for soloists, double choir, organ and orchestra, to a text in Old Church Slavonic. The piece begins and ends with a brass fanfare and contains, in between, an organ solo full of energy. The work is a celebration of Slavic culture and is still often performed today. In pop history it stands far from the charts, but it belongs to the great choral music of the twentieth century, with which the course sketches the music of the century.
artiest/lukas-vasilek.listen: Listen to the organ solo in Janáček's Glagolitic Mass and notice the wild, continuous motion. Can you hear how the choir then comes back in?

artiest/lycourgos-angelopoulos.text:
Lykourgos Angelopoulos was a Greek singer of Byzantine church music. He was born in 1941 in Pyrgos in the Peloponnese and studied Byzantine music at the School of National Music with the musicologist Simon Karas, alongside law at the University of Athens. He became first cantor at the Church of Saint Irene in Athens, founded the Greek Byzantine Choir and taught at conservatories in the city. In 1994 Patriarch Bartholomew I appointed him first chanter of the Patriarchate of Constantinople.

Byzantine music is monophonic. A soloist or a choir sings the melody above a long, sustained note, the ison. The melodies follow fixed modes and are full of ornaments. Angelopoulos published editions of his own using signs from the late Byzantine notation and followed Karas's innovations in his performances. His albums, such as The Byzantine Maestro from 1995 and Hymns from the Holy Mount Athos from 2003, present psalms and hymns from that tradition.

He also became known outside Greece. He contributed to Marcel Pérès's research in France into early Western chant and its connection with Byzantine chant, and with Ensemble Organum he recorded Byzantine, Old Roman and Ambrosian chants. In this way he linked a centuries-old tradition of church singing with the modern world of early music. He died in 2014.
artiest/lycourgos-angelopoulos.listen: Listen to a recording of Byzantine chant and notice the long, sustained note beneath the melody. Can you hear how the singer lets the melody wind around that note?

artiest/lyle-mays.text:
Lyle Mays was an American jazz pianist and composer, best known as a co-founder of the Pat Metheny Group. He was born in 1953 and grew up in rural Wisconsin. His mother played piano and organ, and at the age of nine he was already sitting at the organ at a wedding. Important influences were Bill Evans and the Miles Davis album Filles de Kilimanjaro. He studied at the University of North Texas, wrote there for the One O'Clock Lab Band and then toured for eight months with Woody Herman's big band.

In 1975 he met Pat Metheny at the Wichita jazz festival and shortly afterwards the two founded the Pat Metheny Group. For thirty-three years Mays was the group's pianist, keyboardist, sound designer and composer. Together with Metheny he wrote almost all the music, with which the group won eleven Grammys. Mays played piano, organ and synthesizers, and sometimes accordion or trumpet as well. His own albums include Lyle Mays from 1986, Street Dreams from 1988 and Fictionary from 1993. He also wrote music for children's audiobooks and chamber music.

Mays saw himself more as a contemporary composer than as a jazz pianist. He worked with long forms, harmonically rich and with a broad palette of keyboard colours. After 2010 he no longer performed and worked, among other things, in the software world. He died in 2020.
artiest/lyle-mays.listen: Listen to Distance by the Pat Metheny Group, a piece that Mays wrote for Still Life (Talking). Notice the role of piano and synthesizers alongside the guitar.

artiest/lynyrd-skynyrd.text:
Lynyrd Skynyrd is an American rock band from Jacksonville, Florida. In 1964 singer Ronnie Van Zant, guitarist Gary Rossington and drummer Bob Burns got to know one another through baseball, and with guitarist Allen Collins and bassist Larry Junstrom they started a band. After names such as My Backyard and The One Percent they chose Leonard Skinnerd in 1968, a mocking reference to a gym teacher who made life difficult for boys with long hair. Later that became the idiosyncratic spelling Lynyrd Skynyrd.

In 1972 the producer Al Kooper discovered the band. The debut (Pronounced 'Lĕh-'nérd 'Skin-'nérd) was released in 1973, with Free Bird on it. A tour as the opening act for The Who made the group bigger, and Second Helping (1974) brought the breakthrough with Sweet Home Alabama. That song was an answer to Southern Man by Neil Young, who had criticised the American South. Even so, Young and Van Zant were friends and fans of each other's music. The band blended country, blues and British rock into a southern sound of its own, with three guitarists who alternate and play together.

On 20 October 1977 the band's chartered plane crashed. Ronnie Van Zant, guitarist Steve Gaines and backing singer Cassie Gaines were killed, and the others were seriously injured. In 1987 the band carried on with Ronnie's brother Johnny as singer. Lynyrd Skynyrd made southern rock popular and has been in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame since 2006.
artiest/lynyrd-skynyrd.listen: Listen to Sweet Home Alabama and follow the guitar riff at the start, which runs through almost the whole song. Notice too the female backing vocals and the guitar solos that pop up between the verses.

artiest/m.text:
MØ is the stage name of Karen Marie Ørsted, a Danish singer and songwriter who was born near Odense in 1988 and grew up on the island of Funen. As a child she was captivated by the Spice Girls; as a teenager she listened to punk and to Sonic Youth and Nirvana. She saw Kim Gordon as her great role model. She began in small projects, including with the duo MOR, and signed with Sony Music in 2012.

In 2013 her first single Glass was released, soon followed by Pilgrim and the EP Bikini Daze. In 2014 came the debut album No Mythologies to Follow, with Don't Wanna Dance. That year she also contributed to Iggy Azalea's Beg for It. Her breakthrough to a large audience came in 2015 with Lean On, which she co-wrote and sang for Major Lazer and DJ Snake. It reached number one in several countries. In 2016 came Cold Water, again with Major Lazer, this time with Justin Bieber, and her own Final Song. Later albums are Forever Neverland from 2018, Motordrome from 2022 and Plæygirl from 2025.

Her music combines electronic pop and dance rhythms with a sharp, direct voice and with remnants of the punk she grew up with. MØ shows how a Danish singer, by way of producers and DJs from the world of dance, ended up in international pop.
artiest/m.listen: Listen to Lean On and notice MØ's vocals above the dancing beat. Notice how her voice carries the chorus.

artiest/m-a-r-r-s.text:
M|A|R|R|S was a one-off collaboration from 1987 between two groups on the London label 4AD: Colourbox, the brothers Martyn and Steve Young, and A.R. Kane, Alex Ayuli and Rudy Tambala. The name was formed from the members' first names. That one single showed how you could build a dance record out of pieces of other records.

Pump Up the Volume was recorded at Blackwing Studios, a former church in south London. Martyn Young and engineer John Fryer made a tight house beat. The DJs C.J. Mackintosh and Dave Dorrell then added scratches and samples. The title phrase comes from I Know You Got Soul by Eric B. & Rakim, the oriental vocals of the Israeli singer Ofra Haza come from Im Nin'Alu, and there are drums from Kool & the Gang and the Bar-Kays. The single was released in August 1987 and in October spent two weeks at number 1 in England. It also reached number 1 in the Netherlands, Canada and New Zealand, and number 13 in the United States.

Stock Aitken Waterman took legal action to have a fragment of their Roadblock removed, and for the American release a shout by James Brown was also cut out. Since the early 1990s a sample has had to be cleared in advance. Pump Up the Volume is regarded as one of the first big British house hits and helped make British house and the building of records from samples popular. In April 1988 S'Express reached number 1 in England with Theme from S'Express, also a collage of samples.
artiest/m-a-r-r-s.listen: In Pump Up the Volume, listen to how the track is built like a DJ set: over a steady house beat, new samples keep passing by, such as the title phrase from the rapper Rakim and the high, sped-up vocal fragment from Ofra Haza. Listen too for the scratches: those were added over the top later by DJs.

artiest/m-balamuralikrishna.text:
Mangalampalli Balamuralikrishna was an Indian singer of Carnatic music, the classical music of southern India. He was born in 1930 in Sankaraguptam in what is now the state of Andhra Pradesh. His father was a well-known musician and his mother played the veena. He learned Carnatic music from Parupalli Ramakrishnayya Pantulu, gave his first full concert at the age of eight and was given the nickname Bala, child, by a storyteller. By the age of fifteen he had mastered all seventy-two melakarta ragas and had composed pieces in each of them.

In his life he gave more than twenty-five thousand concerts, in countries such as the United States, France and Russia. He combined classical vocal technique and rhythmic patterns with an audience that wanted to be entertained. He also played the kanjira, mridangam, violin and viola, and introduced the viola into classical Indian music. He sang duets with North Indian musicians such as Bhimsen Joshi and Hariprasad Chaurasia, composed in several languages and ventured into jazz fusion. He also created new ragas, such as Ganapathi and Mahati. Albums such as Raagaanga Ravali from 2006 and Swara Raga Sudha from 2002 let you hear this work.

His awards included the Sangeetha Kalanidhi in 1978 and the Padma Vibhushan in 1991. He died in 2016. For those who follow world music, he is an example of a classical tradition that is open to renewal.
artiest/m-balamuralikrishna.listen: Listen to a recording of Balamuralikrishna and notice how he opens a raga slowly and then ornaments it ever faster and more richly. Can you hear the difference between the free opening and the section with a fixed rhythmic cycle?

artiest/m-beat.text:
M-Beat is the stage name of Marlon Hart, a jungle musician and producer, born in 1975 in East London to Jamaican parents. His father Junior Hart organised parties and in 1988 founded H Jam Productions. An uncle of his is Sly Dunbar, the Jamaican drummer. His father saw him drumming as a schoolboy and gave him an audio workstation.

Jungle is a style from London with fast breakbeats and heavy basslines. The breakthrough came in 1994 with Incredible, a collaboration with the reggae singer General Levy, which reached the top ten in the United Kingdom. The track was performed on Top of the Pops. That same year came Sweet Love, an adaptation of a song by Anita Baker with the singer Nazlyn and trumpeter Kenny Wellington. In 1996 he worked with Jamiroquai on Do U Know Where You're Coming From.

M-Beat showed how jungle could be connected with reggae and reach the charts. The genre came out of London's club life.
artiest/m-beat.listen: Listen to Incredible and notice the fast breakbeat and the bassline. Where do you hear the reggae in it?

artiest/m-s-subbulakshmi.text: M.S. Subbulakshmi from Madurai sang at the Music Academy in Madras at the age of thirteen and became the best-known voice of Carnatic music. In 1945 she played the poet-saint Meera in the film Meera. In 1966 she became the first Indian to sing at the United Nations, and in 1998 she became the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna. Her recording of the Suprabhatam (1963) is still played every morning in homes and temples.
artiest/m-s-subbulakshmi.listen: Listen to the Suprabhatam, a morning song to wake the god Venkateswara: hear how calmly and evenly she recites the Sanskrit verses.

artiest/ma-rainey.text: Gertrude 'Ma' Rainey performed from the beginning of the twentieth century in minstrel and tent shows in the South and sang the blues there long before it reached records. She became known as the 'Mother of the Blues'. Between 1923 and 1928 she recorded almost a hundred songs for Paramount, with accompanists such as Louis Armstrong and the pianist Thomas Dorsey. Her voice was deep and powerful, and her lyrics were about love, infidelity and life on the road. In Prove It on Me Blues she sang openly about love between women. When the record market collapsed in the Depression, she went back to Columbus, Georgia, where she died in 1939.
artiest/ma-rainey.listen: Notice how the singing sits behind the beat and lets every line ring out just as late.

artiest/machito.text: The singer and maracas player Francisco 'Machito' Grillo grew up in Havana and moved to New York in 1937. In 1940 he founded Machito & His Afro-Cubans; his brother-in-law, the trumpeter Mario Bauzá, became the musical director. Bauzá had played in jazz orchestras and wanted to combine Cuban rhythms with jazz arrangements. The result was Tanga (1943). The band played in dance halls such as the Palladium Ballroom and became the model for Latin orchestras. Jazz soloists such as Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and Cannonball Adderley recorded with Machito; Parker played on Chico O'Farrill's Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite in 1950. Machito kept performing until his death in 1984, most recently in London.
artiest/machito.listen: Listen to the percussion section beneath the big band: congas, bongos and timbales.

artiest/machito-and-his-afro-cubans.text:
Machito and His Afro-Cubans was a big band in New York that combined Afro-Cuban rhythms with jazz arrangements. Frank Grillo, known as Machito, grew up in Havana. About his birth he himself gave varying accounts, sometimes Havana, sometimes Tampa in Florida. In 1937 he came to New York as a singer and played with Latin orchestras and with the bandleader Xavier Cugat. On 3 December 1940 he held the first rehearsal of the Afro-Cubans in a ballroom in Harlem. A few weeks later his brother-in-law Mario Bauzá became musical director, a role he held for thirty-four years.

The line-up was that of a big band, with trumpets and saxophones, supplemented with piano, bass, drums and Cuban bongos. Machito stood in front of the group and played the maracas. Bauzá determined the character and brought in arrangers from the jazz world. As early as 1941 the band had a hit with Sopa de Pichon, a joke among Puerto Rican immigrants about nearly starving in New York. The singer Graciela, Machito's foster sister, sang on many recordings. In 1975 Machito opted for a smaller line-up and toured widely in Europe, with his son and daughter in the band. In 1983 he received a Grammy, a year before his death.

The Afro-Cubans are regarded as pioneers of Cubop and of Latin jazz, and later of salsa. Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, George Shearing and Stan Kenton cited the band as an influence. In East Harlem an intersection bears the name Machito Square.
artiest/machito-and-his-afro-cubans.listen: Listen to Sopa de Pichon and notice how the big band's brass plays together with bongos and percussion. Try to hear what comes from the Cuban tradition and what from the jazz tradition.

artiest/machito-en-his-afro-cubans.text:
Machito and his Afro-Cubans was a Latin jazz band, founded in 1940 by Machito. The musical director was Mario Bauzá, Machito's brother-in-law. The group combined Cuban music with orchestrations that came out of swing.

After a few early recordings for Decca, the orchestra became better known towards the end of the Second World War, when it performed with Stan Kenton's orchestra. Machito played maracas on Kenton's recordings of The Peanut Vendor and Cuban Carnival. The group then recorded for Mercury and Clef. At Bauzá's insistence, American jazz soloists joined in on the recordings between 1948 and 1960, among them Howard McGhee, Harry Edison and Cannonball Adderley.

The Afro-Cubans played with Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Flip Phillips and Buddy Rich. The influence went both ways: the orchestra's Latin rhythms had a great influence on the New York jazz scene. In this way Machito brought Cuban percussion and jazz improvisation together.
artiest/machito-en-his-afro-cubans.listen: Listen to Tanga and notice the percussion with congas and bongos beneath the horns. How do the horns respond to it?

artiest/macintosh-plus.text:
Macintosh Plus is one of the stage names of Ramona Andra Langley, an American electronic musician. She also releases music as Vektroid, dstnt, Laserdisc Visions, New Dreams Ltd., Virtual Information Desk and PrismCorp Virtual Enterprises. She began making and releasing electronic music in 2005 and has by now put out more than forty releases.

With her ninth studio album, Floral Shoppe from 2011, she played, as Macintosh Plus, a major role in the rise of vaporwave. The album includes, among other things, リサフランク420 / 現代のコンピュー. Fact called Floral Shoppe the defining album of Bandcamp, the service on which Langley releases her music. It is the most recommended album in the experimental music category on that site. Tiny Mix Tapes included the album in a list of favourites in 2012. From early 2013 she released music less often.

Vaporwave is an electronic style that emerged between 2010 and 2013. Macintosh Plus and New Dreams Ltd. are regarded as the most important projects of the genre. Critics read in her work a critique of late capitalism. In this way Langley became a key figure in a musical movement that arose on the internet.
artiest/macintosh-plus.listen: Listen to リサフランク420 / 現代のコンピュー and notice the slow tempo and the repetition. What atmosphere emerges?

artiest/mack-gordon.text:
Mack Gordon was an American lyricist for stage and screen. He was born in 1904 as Morris Gittler in Grodno, which then belonged to the Russian Empire and now lies in Belarus. In 1907 he emigrated with his mother and brother to the United States, where his father lived in New Jersey. In the late 1920s and early 1930s he performed in vaudeville as an actor and singer, but his talent lay in writing song lyrics. For Broadway he made, among other things, the revue Fast and Furious in 1931.

In the 1930s he worked with the English pianist Harry Revel. In the 1940s he wrote with other composers, including Harry Warren. His name appears on the music of more than a hundred films, for at least fifty of which he wrote specially. He was nominated nine times for an Oscar for Best Song, five years in a row from 1940 to 1944, and won with You'll Never Know. At Last and The More I See You also belong to his lasting work. They were sung by, among others, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole, Etta James and Barbra Streisand and are still heard in films and commercials.

Gordon was active in the Hollywood branch of the copyright organisation ASCAP. He died in 1959. His songs show how the lyrics of the film musical filled the repertoire of pop singers for decades.
artiest/mack-gordon.listen: Listen to At Last in the version by Etta James and notice how the lyrics and the long melodic lines reinforce one another. Can you hear how a song from a 1940s film could later become a soul classic?

artiest/madlib.text:
Madlib is the stage name of Otis Jackson Jr., an American DJ, producer and rapper, born in 1973 in Oxnard, California. His parents were musicians and his uncle is the jazz trumpeter Jon Faddis. At eleven he sampled his first track, from his father's records. In the 1990s he worked with rappers in his studio, and with Lootpack he made records for Stones Throw. His first solo album, The Unseen from 2000, was released under the name Quasimoto.

In 2001 he began the Yesterdays New Quintet series, a jazz group in which Madlib himself is all the players. In 2003 Shades of Blue appeared, for which he delved into the Blue Note archive, and with J Dilla he formed the duo Jaylib. With MF Doom he made, as Madvillain, the album Madvillainy from 2004. Freddie Gibbs' Piñata followed in 2014 and Bandana in 2019. In 2010 he started his own label, Madlib Invazion.

His production style makes extensive use of samples from sources both obscure and well known. His greatest examples are Miles Davis, Sun Ra and David Axelrod. His work often contains elements of jazz and world music. This has earned him a reputation as one of the most influential producers in modern hip hop.
artiest/madlib.listen: Listen to Mystic Bounce and notice the samples, the beat and the bass. Which jazz sounds do you hear in it, and how are they stuck together?

artiest/madness.text:
Madness is an English ska and pop band from Camden Town in north London. The core began in 1976 as the North London Invaders, with Mike Barson on keyboards, Chris Foreman on guitar and Lee Thompson on saxophone. In 1977 Graham McPherson, known as Suggs, took over the vocals. After a short spell under the name Morris and the Minors, the band was called Madness in 1979, after a song by Prince Buster, one of their great role models. With Chas Smash as the seventh member, for backing vocals and dance, the line-up was complete.

Their first record, The Prince, came out on 2 Tone Records, the label of Jerry Dammers of The Specials. Madness toured with The Specials and The Selecter and released their debut album One Step Beyond... in 1979, with the singles One Step Beyond and My Girl. Baggy Trousers, Our House, House of Fun and It Must Be Love followed. From 1980 to 1986 was their most successful period; after that came albums such as Keep Moving, The Liberty of Norton Folgate from 2009 and Can't Touch Us Now from 2016. In 2000 they received the Ivor Novello Award for their entire songbook.

Their sound combines the rhythm of ska with British pop melodies and the humour of the streets of London. Madness turned the Two-Tone wave into a broad pop movement and continues to perform with six of the seven original members.
artiest/madness.listen: Listen to One Step Beyond and notice the ska rhythm, the saxophone and the spoken intro. Can you hear how the beat is accented on the second and fourth beats throughout?

artiest/madonna.text:
Madonna Louise Ciccone was born in Bay City, Michigan, in 1958 and grew up in the suburbs of Detroit. She first took piano lessons, but chose ballet. In 1978 she dropped out of her studies and moved to New York to break through as a dancer and musician. She sang, drummed and played guitar in the rock bands Breakfast Club and Emmy. In 1982 she persuaded DJs in the clubs to play her demo. DJ Mark Kamins of the club Danceteria put her in touch with Sire Records, where her first single Everybody was released.

She broke through with the debut album Madonna (1983). Like a Virgin (1984), True Blue (1986) and Like a Prayer (1989) followed. Her music came out of the dance clubs of New York: danceable pop with synthesizers and drum machines. Hits such as Like a Virgin, Papa Don't Preach, La Isla Bonita, Like a Prayer and Vogue made her, together with Michael Jackson and Prince, one of the biggest stars of the 1980s. She co-wrote her songs, also produced herself and kept coming up with a new look. Later she continued to reinvent herself, with the electronic albums Ray of Light (1998) and Music (2000) and the disco record Confessions on a Dance Floor (2005).

Madonna also acted in films, such as Desperately Seeking Susan and Evita, and had her own record label in Maverick. Her work often deals with sex, religion and politics, which brought admiration and uproar. She broke boundaries for women in pop music: she decided for herself about her music and her image, and so she became a role model for many later pop stars.
artiest/madonna.listen: Listen to Material Girl. Notice the tight synthesizer bass and the drum machine beneath the vocals, and how few real instruments can actually be heard.

artiest/maelstrom-percussion-ensemble.text:
Maelström Percussion Ensemble is a percussion ensemble that focuses on the repertoire of modern music. Nothing was found in our sources about its founding or its membership, so what follows is only what the albums show.

Three recordings are known: Imaginary Landscapes from 1996, Labrynth from 2000 and Pika-Don from 2004. The first title refers to John Cage's Imaginary Landscapes series, written for percussion and electronics. That fits a group that feels at home in the experimental classical music of the twentieth century, in which percussion takes a leading role of its own. An ensemble of percussionists sounds different from an orchestra: there are no long melodic lines, but sound, rhythm, silence and colour. Marimbas, drums, cymbals, gongs and unusual objects together form a palette that is above all about texture.

Such ensembles are important for pop history because they brought percussion out of the background. Rock drummers and producers of electronic music found in the work of Cage and his contemporaries ideas about sound as material.
artiest/maelstrom-percussion-ensemble.listen: Listen to a piece by a percussion ensemble and pay attention not to melody but to timbre: which instruments do you hear, and how does the sound change when the manner of playing changes?
